one_liner: Nim 2.2.12 ref objects (default ORC, Nim's own allocator) build and free depth-20 trees 1.35x faster than the best make_unique C++ build.
what_it_does: This is a row from LangArena, a 50-task, 26-language benchmark suite, not a library. Binarytrees::Obj builds a complete depth-20 binary tree (2,097,151 nodes), sums it recursively and lets it go, 30 times in the timed loop after 6 warm-up iterations. The Nim version (nim/src/benchmarks/binarytrees.nim) makes each node a `ref object` with left and right refs and a 64-bit int item, and ARC/ORC destroys the whole tree when run() returns. The checksum 75497436 (36 x 2,097,151) is checked for every language. To get the speedup you write the allocation-heavy part in Nim with plain ref objects; nothing links into a C++ program.
how_it_is_fast: The difference is in allocation and freeing, not in the loop code. Nim's nimNewObj allocates from Nim's own allocator (lib/system/alloc.nim): a thread-local region with page-sized small chunks in 16-byte size classes. An allocation pops the chunk's free list or bumps an accumulator, and a free pushes the cell back onto its chunk's free list; the source says 'true deallocation is delayed for as long as possible in favor of reusing cells'. ARC/ORC frees the tree with a recursive destructor at scope end, using non-atomic RC operations (doc/mm.md). The C and C++ versions instead call glibc malloc/free (C++ through std::make_unique and the unique_ptr destructor) once per 24-byte node. Per node that comes to 24.6 ns for Nim/Clang (ORC), 19.0 ns for Nim/GCC/ARC, 33.3 ns for C++/G++/Fast and 39.5 ns for C/Clang (derived from page data over 62.9M timed nodes). This mechanism is an inference from the sources; the suite does not explain the result.
when_to_use: Nim programs that build and drop many small heap nodes (ASTs, tries, temporary trees) with plain ref objects: the stock allocator plus ARC/ORC beat per-node new/malloc C++ and C by 1.35x (ORC, prod) to 1.76x (ARC) here.
Acyclic structures where you can build with --mm:arc: the ARC rows (1.193 s gcc, 1.214 s clang) use about the same peak memory as C++ (69 MB vs 70 MB) and are still 1.7x faster.

Deciding whether to port tree-heavy Nim code to C++ for speed: idiomatic make_unique C++ and malloc C lost in all 27 C and C++ rows (20 gcc and clang configurations plus the mycc and cproc hobby compilers; 2.081-2.548 s, and 3.65 s for the instrumented C/Gcc/PGO/Gen build) unless it switches to an arena.
Any Nim backend: every Nim row on this test (gcc, clang, the nim cpp C++ backend at 1.494-1.523 s, NLVM at 1.385 s) is faster than the best C/C++ row.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Nim beats C or C++ with an arena: the suite's realloc-grown C index arena takes 0.255 s (C/Gcc/Fast, 27 MB) and the C++ std::vector arena 0.512-0.685 s, while Nim's own seq-based arena variant takes 1.049 s at 235 MB.
Memory-constrained code on the default ORC: peak RSS is 102 MB vs 70 MB for C++ (about 46 percent more), because each ORC cell is 48 bytes against a 32-byte malloc chunk (derived, see gotchas).
Comparisons against C or C++ linked with a fast allocator (mimalloc, jemalloc, a pool): not measured; the baseline is glibc malloc in the suite's ubuntu:26.04 containers.
Builds that need -d:useMalloc (Valgrind, sanitizers) replace Nim's allocator with the C one; not measured, and the gap should shrink since the allocator is the likely source of the win (inference).
Cyclic object graphs with the faster ARC setting: ARC leaks cycles and the docs say async code needs ORC, so the 1.76x figure only holds for acyclic data.

integration.dependencies: Nim 2.2.12 compiler plus a C compiler (clang 22.1.8 from the LLVM release tarball for the prod row, gcc 16 trunk for the ARC row); the tree code uses only Nim's system module, while the suite's harness also needs the jsony and regex nimble packages
integration.min_toolchain: Nim 2.2.12 as measured (nimble file requires nim >= 2.0.0); ORC is the default memory manager in the v2.2.12 doc/mm.md; older Nim versions were not measured
integration.platforms: Measured on x86-64 Linux (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 78 GB) in Docker images built FROM ubuntu:26.04 with a 16 GB memory limit; the build targets generic x86-64 (no -march=native)
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable: single-threaded workload built with --threads:on; ARC/ORC RC operations are non-atomic and object subgraphs are moved between threads rather than shared (doc/mm.md)

gotchas: The default ORC row pays for cycle collection the tree does not need. TreeNodeObj has no {.acyclic.} annotation, and Nim's ORC announcement post says this annotation 'can be crucial in order to get ORC's performance close to ARC's'. ORC also adds a rootIdx word to every object header (lib/system/arc.nim RefHeader). With a 24-byte payload and MemAlign 16, that makes 48-byte ORC cells against 32-byte ARC cells: 2,097,151 x 48 B = 100.7 MB and x 32 B = 67.1 MB, which matches the measured 102 MB and 69 MB (derived). The headline 1.76x comes from the non-default ARC 'hack' row; the default prod row gives 1.35x.

The harness looks fair on work done. C frees every node in a separate pass and C++ through recursive unique_ptr destructors inside each timed iteration, and Nim's destructor runs at the end of run(); the 69 MB peak of the ARC row shows only one tree is alive at a time. The Nim harness calls GC_fullCollect() after warm-up and after the timer, but under ARC/ORC an acyclic tree that has already been freed gives that call nothing to collect. Depth and iteration counts are read from run.js at runtime.

The flags and types are not matched. Nim's -d:release maps to clang -O3 or gcc -O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno, both with -fno-strict-aliasing (v2.2.12 config/nim.cfg), and keeps overflow and bound checks on. The C/C++ prod rows are -O2 with -fstack-protector-strong, but the -O3 -march=native Fast, -ffast-math Unsafe and PGO rows also lose (2.098-2.457 s). The Nim node holds a 64-bit int item where C and C++ use a 32-bit int.

Each configuration is timed once per monthly run, with no repeats. The lead held in all five runs checked (2026-07-14 to 2026-10-05: Nim/Clang 1.513-1.564 s vs C++/G++ 2.101-2.21 s), including the 2026-10-05 run after the host OS moved from Ubuntu to Arch Linux (the containers stay ubuntu:26.04).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: This is stronger evidence than the benchLANG Nim binary-trees sibling (one run, compile-time constant inputs, 1.25x vs C): it measures 20 gcc and clang C/C++ build configurations, ARC, ORC and backend variants, and an arena variant over five monthly runs. Unlike the Koka cfold and deriv siblings, the C++ baseline here really frees its nodes. Java's Binarytrees::Obj row is 3.2x faster (0.479 s) but peaks at 892 MB, so pick Nim when deterministic freeing and 69-102 MB matter.
verified_claims_summary: LangArena's 2026-10-05 run on an AMD Ryzen 7 3800X (Linux, Docker) timed 30 depth-20 build-sum-free iterations. Nim 2.2.12 (nim c -d:release --cc:clang, clang 22.1.8 at -O3, default ORC, Nim's allocator) took 1.55 s and the Nim/GCC/ARC build 1.193 s. The best C/C++ configuration, C++/G++/Fast (GCC 16.0.1 trunk, -O3 -march=native, std::make_unique nodes, glibc malloc), took 2.098 s and the prod C++/G++ row 2.101 s. That is about 1.35x and 1.76x (derived from page data), with every checksum matching 75497436.
status_note: Nim is actively developed (MIT with some modules excepted, 18.3k stars, 23,330 commits on devel), and LangArena is an active MIT suite (41 stars, last commit 2026-10-08, monthly reruns); the 20-line tree code is copyable, but the win belongs to Nim's runtime allocator and ARC/ORC, not to the source.
